name: no-more-secrets
desc: Recreates the SETEC ASTRONOMY effect from 'Sneakers'
why: Recreates the Sneakers decoding effect in the terminal; a fun visual toy with a little history behind it.

brief.what_it_is: No More Secrets is a command-line tool, nms, that recreates the decryption effect from the 1992 movie Sneakers. It takes ASCII or UTF-8 text piped in on stdin and prints it to the terminal, first showing scrambled characters and then running a decryption sequence that reveals the original text. A second program, sneakers, reproduces the specific clip from the movie and waits for the user to choose a menu option before it exits. The project has no dependencies by default and uses ANSI/VT100 escape sequences for the effect.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as recreating the famous on-screen data decryption effect from Sneakers (the clip is at 0:35 of the linked YouTube video). The author also offers the effect as a C library, LibNMS, for other command-line programs.
brief.how_it_works: By default, nms draws the piped text as encrypted characters and waits for a key press before starting the decryption sequence; the -a flag starts it automatically. The effect is drawn with ANSI/VT100 terminal escape sequences, and an ncurses build is provided for terminals that do not support them. The README does not describe the scrambling algorithm itself.

commands_seen.context: Builds the nms binary from the cloned source (git clone, then cd into the repo).
Optional build step for the sneakers program that recreates the movie clip.
Installs the built binaries system-wide after building.
Basic usage: pipe a directory listing into nms to see the effect.
Uses the -a flag to start decryption automatically without a key press.
Uses the -s flag to mask single space characters.
Uses the -f flag to set the decrypted text's foreground color to green.
Uses the -c flag to clear the screen before output and restore it afterward.
Prints the version, useful for checking a package-manager install is current.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, the README describes building from source. You need git, gcc, and make. Clone https://github.com/bartobri/no-more-secrets.git, then run make nms, optionally make sneakers, and sudo make install. For terminals without ANSI/VT100 support, the README describes an ncurses build (make nms-ncurses and make sneakers-ncurses) that needs the ncurses library, with installation steps in a NCURSES.md file in the repo. The README also says several Unix/Linux package managers include the project, and recommends checking nms -v against the latest version. No runtime configuration or first-run steps are mentioned.
brief.standout: It is a small C tool that reproduces a single movie visual exactly, and it doubles as a reusable library (LibNMS) for other command-line programs. The effect works on any piped text, so it can be applied to ordinary command output.
brief.status: Appears maintained but I could not confirm recency. The README badge shows version 1.0.2, and the README says several Unix/Linux package managers ship it. The fetched README shows no release date or last-commit timestamp, and I did not check the commit history or release page.
brief.caveats: Relies on ANSI/VT100 escape sequences, so terminals without support may render the effect badly; the ncurses fallback loses inline output and always clears the screen. Input must be ASCII or UTF-8 text. With -c, nms waits for a key press before restoring the terminal. The sneakers program exits only after a menu option is selected. Building from source needs git, gcc, and make, and the ncurses build needs the ncurses library. Licensed under GPL, per the README. The brew caveats field is empty.
quotes: This command works on piped data. Pipe any ASCII or UTF-8 text to `nms`, and it will apply the Hollywood effect, initially showing encrypted data, then starting a decryption sequence to reveal the original plain-text characters.
recreates the famous data decryption effect seen on screen in the 1992 hacker movie Sneakers.
For those who would like to use this effect in their own projects, I have created a C library that provides simple interface and can easily be used for any program that runs from the command line.
